newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope gets tumultuous welcome in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Pope gets tumultuous welcome in Lebanon.

text.p: Crowds throwing rice and rose petals and waving yellow-and-white papal flags gave Pope John Paul a tumultuous welcome on Saturday at the start of a brief visit to Lebanon, his first to a Middle Eastern country.

Tens of thousands of people waving flags, balloons and even tree branches greeted the pontiff as he drove through Beirut on a flag-decked 10-km (six-mile) route from the airport to the presidential palace.
The pope's welcome was far more enthusiastic, and the crowds were far larger, than a month ago on his pilgrimage of reconciliation to Sarajevo, the Bosnian capital.
In the first speech of his 32-hour visit, the 76-year-old pontiff said he had come to Lebanon as a friend to encourage its sons and daughters, "so desirous of independence and freedom".
Without naming Syria or Israel, he issued a veiled call for the departure of 35,000 Syrian troops stationed in the country and 2,000 Israeli troops who hold a border occupation zone in south Lebanon.
John Paul said he had frequently alerted the international community "to help the Lebanese people to once again find peace in a national territory recognised and respected by all".

Many of Lebanon's Christian minority demand the departure of the Syrians and accuse the Beirut government of surrendering its powers of decision to Syria's leaders, while most Moslems see the departure of the Israelis as their top priority.
The government, whose members consult Syria on most issues, says it needs Syria's backing to maintain security in the country and closely aligns its anti-Israeli policies with Syria.

Women along the road ululated and shouted "Alleluia", men released white doves and children darted past soldiers to run beside the bulletproof "Popemobile" as the pope drove through Moslem and Christian quarters of the Lebanese capital.
The turnout was big and enthusiastic in Christian districts with crowds lining the road several deep and packing balconies, but many people also turned out in Moslem districts.
Shi'ite women in full-length black chadors worn by fundamentalists waved red-and-black Shi'ite flags as the pope drove past.
"I believe he is here to talk about peace and this is why I came out to welcome him," said Faten Najdi, an 11-year-old girl. "It's true he's Christian, but he is for all the people."

Church bells rang out across Lebanon and a 21-gun salute boomed as the pope landed at Beirut airport, walked slowly down the steps of the plane and stooped as if to kiss a box of Lebanese soil held up by two children.

Hundreds of civil dignitaries and Moslem and Christian clerics greeted John Paul at the airport, heavily guarded by troops carrying automatic rifles backed by helicopters overhead and Lebanese navy gunboats patrolling the sea nearby.
President Elias Hrawi, a Maronite Christian, told the pope he was "the image of hope for all the Lebanese people".

Hrawi said in a welcoming speech that Lebanon, which underwent a 1975-90 sectarian civil war from which the Christian minority emerged defeated, was trying to consolidate a system defending freedom of belief and dignity for all its people.

Billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, a Sunni Moslem, told Reuters he believed the pope's visit would help "national consolidation". "It will give Christians more confidence in themselves and their country," he said.
The pope is known to regard Lebanon, the only Arab country that grants equality to all its people, Moslem and Christian alike, as an example in a region where Christian communities are in decline.

But many Lebanese Christians complain that they have been marginalised from politics since the civil war, while others refuse to participate because they believe the pro-Syrian government will not give them a fair deal.
John Paul's message was that all Lebanese should be committed to peace and reconciliation, and all should be given an equal opportunity.

"In this new Lebanon which you are slowly rebuilding, it is important to give a place to every citizen," he said, "particularly those who, inspired by legitimate patriotism, wish to become involved in political activity or economic life.
"From this point of view, the first condition for any truly democratic process is a just balance between the vital forces of the nation...," he added.
